claims.claim: REMOVED, the sweep’s worst finding on this page (F-FAIL, independently re-confirmed): "limited amounts of legislation on the Consent Calendar." The House Rules and Manual for the 119th Congress carries "Sec. 899. Former Consent Calendar. For the former Consent Calendar rule, see Sec. 899 of the House Rules and Manual for the 111th Congress (H. Doc. 110-162)" - the calendar is not operative, so the article’s present tense was wrong. Replaced with the Manual’s own pointer, the parallel Former Corrections Calendar entry, and the route the House actually uses for measures that draw no real opposition: suspension of the rules under clause 1 of Rule XV, which is a two-thirds VOTE and not consent at all.

REMOVED, F-FAIL (sweep finding, independently re-confirmed twice - against the stored corpus snapshot AND against data/cache.json in this session): "The Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2025 (S. 1884) passed both chambers this way, reflecting the absence of any senator willing to formally oppose it." The record shows two different methods: Senate 2025-12-10 Passed (Unanimous Consent), House 2026-03-16 Passed (Voice Vote). The page now states both and says in terms that a voice vote is not unanimous consent. The trailing motive clause ("reflecting the absence of any senator willing to formally oppose it") was also removed as unsourced motive attribution. NOTE FOR A LATER BATCH: articles/holocaust-art-recovery.html carries the same error about the same bill and is NOT in this batch.

REMOVED and REPLACED with the opposite of what it implied: "The Senate confirms hundreds of nominations per Congress... The majority leadership periodically seeks UC to confirm large batches of lower-profile nominations without individual votes." The count was uncited and low; the mechanism was uncited and, on the record, wrong. Congress.gov’s 119th-Congress nomination records show 1,622 confirmations, of which 1,034 are recorded as VOICE VOTE and 588 as YEA-NAY VOTE, and NONE as unanimous consent. This is the same voice-vote-is-not-unanimous-consent confusion as the S. 1884 error, on the same page.

REMOVED, unsourced procedural-equivalence claim: "A UC agreement that limits debate to four hours accomplishes the same result as invoking cloture - without the days of procedural delay and the formal 60-vote threshold." No stored source states the equivalence, and the four-hour figure is invented. Replaced with CRS’s own careful phrase - complex agreements "are a form of voluntary cloture" - and with RS22299’s statement of the actual relationship: proceeding to a measure is a vote, cloture, or unanimous consent, and without clearance the motion to proceed "is debatable and therefore may be filibustered."

FIXED, the sweep’s F-UNSOURCED #5: the page used "unanimous consent agreement" and "UC request" interchangeably and drew no distinction. CRS 98-225 draws it explicitly - "It is worth distinguishing between simple unanimous consent requests and complex unanimous consent agreements" - and the page now has a section on it with the source’s own examples of each.

REMOVED, unsourced share claim in the meta description and echoed in the body: "Most Senate business - and much House business - moves through unanimous consent agreements rather than formal votes." No stored source gives a share, and nothing supports the House half at all; the House claim is also in tension with what this audit found about the House (suspension of the rules, a two-thirds vote). Replaced with CRS’s own framing, that the Senate is fundamentally a unanimous-consent institution whose rules are set aside regularly and whose members propound requests every day it is in session.

REPLACED, sweep F-UNSOURCED: the hold was defined as "an informal signal of intent to object to any UC request... doesn’t have formal procedural standing." Now sourced to CRS R43563 and RL30360, and corrected in one respect: the standing rules do not address the practice, but the Senate HAS adopted notification requirements (P.L. 110-81 section 512 in 2007, and a 112th-Congress standing order), under which a hold is formally a "notice of intent to object to proceeding" and becomes public if certain criteria are met. The hold taxonomy (informational, choke, blanket) is added from the same source.

REMOVED, unsourced: "because the House has 435 members and operates under strict time rules managed by the Rules Committee, it’s less central to House operations than it is to the Senate", and "Most significant House business flows through the Rules Committee and formal floor procedures, not UC." No stored source supports either the membership figure in this context or the comparative claim. Replaced with what the House Rules and Manual itself records about unanimous consent in the House.

REMOVED, unsourced editorialising: "unanimous consent is what makes it possible to conduct any business at all"; "This gives individual senators significant leverage"; "Senators use this leverage strategically... is a way of extracting concessions." Each replaced with a sourced statement or dropped. CRS’s own version of the last one - that leaders honour holds because refusing risks a filibuster that consumes scarce floor time - is now quoted instead.

MOVED, not removed: "inserting materials into the Congressional Record" was listed as House use of UC. The stored source that lists it (CRS 98-225) lists it among the SENATE’s simple unanimous consent requests, and the stored CR user’s guide says only that "In the Senate, with unanimous consent, undelivered remarks are printed as if spoken." It now appears in the Senate list, where the source puts it.
